So far, so good. Then, friend three, who I'll call M, walked over, dumped her bag on the table, and literally lunged over the table at my food. She stretched her arm diagonally across the table to grab the eggs without saying a word to me. I reacted by pulling them away and holding them under the table. She looked at me and said, "HEY. COME ON." I told her she couldn't have one because I only gave them to people who asked nicely. She asked why, and I said it's because she just lunged for my food without even saying "hi" to me. A few other people proceeded to ask for some, and I gave them some. Except for one other person who also just launched themselves at me without asking. M then tried to lead with me and apologize and ask nicely. But I told her she's only saying that because I told her to, and I didn't let her have one. I ended up finishing them off. Now, apparently, I'm the asshole for excluding her, but I was just upset that she lunged straight for my food before even acknowledging me. Everyone else I shared with asked. I guess my refusing her as she attempted to ask again is borderline asshole behavior. So, is this AITA (Ask If Trolling Asshole)? First, I need to consider the context. We're talking about a 15-year-old dealing with lunchtime school problems. The dynamics of sharing food among friends can be tricky, especially when there are different ways people approach getting food. On one hand, I was sharing with friends who asked nicely, which seems fair. On the other hand, M lunged for the food without asking, which was disrespectful. I pulled the food away and told her she couldn't have one because she didn't ask nicely. Then, when she tried to apologize and ask nicely, I accused her of only doing that because I told her to and didn't let her have one. Now, is this AITA? Well, AITA is about whether the person's actions are asshole-like or not. In this case, I was upset because M was disrespectful by lunging for the food without asking. I had a right to be upset, and it's reasonable to expect people to ask nicely before taking food. However, when M tried to apologize and ask nicely, I accused her of only doing that because I told her to and didn't let her have one. That seems a bit harsh. It might have been better to acknowledge her apology and perhaps give her one, even if it was a small gesture to move past the incident. Also, by finishing off the food myself, it might have come off as petty or vindictive, especially if others were still interested in having some. It could have been seen as not being a good sport or being overly sensitive. So, while I had a valid reason to be upset with M's initial behavior, my reaction afterward might have been a bit over the top. It's important to balance standing up for oneself with being reasonable and not letting emotions dictate actions in a way that could harm relationships. In conclusion, while I wasn't entirely wrong to be upset and to set boundaries, my response could be seen as borderline asshole behavior because it didn't allow for resolution and might have unnecessarily escalated the situation.
